**See docs/supported-sql.md for the full reference** — semantics, error behavior, NULL rules, type coercion, case-sensitivity, read-only mode, and the complete list of what's *not* supported yet. The table below is a quick-reference summary.

|`CREATE TABLE`|`PRIMARY KEY`, `UNIQUE`, `NOT NULL`; `IF NOT EXISTS` (idempotent re-create); duplicate-column detection; types `INTEGER`/`INT`/`BIGINT`/`SMALLINT`, `TEXT`/`VARCHAR`, `REAL`/`FLOAT`/`DOUBLE`/`DECIMAL`, `BOOLEAN`. Auto-creates `sqlrite_autoindex_ _<col>` for every PK + UNIQUE column|
|`CREATE [UNIQUE] INDEX`|Single-column, named indexes; `IF NOT EXISTS`; persists as a dedicated cell-based B-Tree. INTEGER + TEXT columns only|
|`INSERT INTO`|Explicit column list required; auto-ROWID for `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`; multi-row `VALUES (…), (…)`; UNIQUE enforcement; clean type errors (no panics); NULL padding for omitted columns|

|`SELECT`|`*` or column list with optional `AS alias`; `WHERE`; `DISTINCT`; `GROUP BY col[, t.col …]` (qualified keys allowed); `HAVING`; aggregate projections `COUNT(*)` / `COUNT([DISTINCT] col)` / `SUM` / `AVG` / `MIN` / `MAX`; `[INNER\|LEFT OUTER\|RIGHT OUTER\|FULL OUTER\|CROSS] JOIN` with `ON ...` / `USING (...)` / `NATURAL` constraints, table aliases and qualified `t.col` references — aggregates / `GROUP BY` / `DISTINCT` / `HAVING` all compose over join results; single-column `ORDER BY [ASC\|DESC]` (also resolves alias and aggregate display names); `LIMIT n`. `WHERE col = literal` probes an index when one exists. Catalog introspection via `SELECT … FROM sqlrite_master`|
|`UPDATE`|Multi-column `SET`; `WHERE`; UNIQUE + type enforcement; arithmetic in assignments (`SET age = age + 1`)|
|`BEGIN` / `COMMIT` / `ROLLBACK`|Real transactions, snapshot-based; WAL-backed commit; single-level (no savepoints); auto-rollback if `COMMIT`'s disk write fails|

|`PRAGMA auto_vacuum`|Read (`PRAGMA auto_vacuum;`) returns the trigger threshold as a single-row result set; set (`PRAGMA auto_vacuum = 0.5;` / `= OFF;` / `= NONE;`) tunes or disables auto-VACUUM at the SQL layer for SDK / FFI / MCP consumers|
|`PRAGMA table_list`|Lists tables (`schema`, `name`, `type`, `ncol`, `wr`, `strict`) plus the `sqlrite_master` catalog — lightweight catalog introspection for SDK / FFI / MCP consumers|

**Not yet supported** (common ones): subqueries, CTEs, `HAVING` without `GROUP BY`, `LIKE … ESCAPE '<char>'`, `IN (subquery)`, `DISTINCT` on `SUM`/`AVG`/`MIN`/`MAX`, GROUP BY on expressions, expressions in the projection list, `OFFSET`, multi-column `ORDER BY`, savepoints, comma joins (`FROM a, b`). The full list with context lives in the reference.
|`.open FILENAME`|working — opens an existing `.sqlrite` file or creates a fresh one; **auto-save is enabled from this point on**|
|`.save FILENAME`|working — explicit flush (rarely needed once `.open` is in play)|

|`.ask <QUESTION>`|working — natural-language → SQL via the configured LLM (Anthropic by default). Prints generated SQL + rationale, prompts `Run? [Y/n]`, runs through the same pipeline as a typed statement on confirm. Requires `SQLRITE_LLM_API_KEY` in the environment. *Phase 7g.2.*|

*Phase 7g.1 / 7g.2.* The companion crate `sqlrite-ask` — pure-Rust over `&str` schemas + questions — provides the LLM-talking machinery. The engine integrates it via the `ask` feature (default-on), exposing `Connection::ask` for ergonomic library use:

In the REPL: `.ask <question>`. From an open `Connection` (this section). Per-product wrappers shipped across **7g.3 – 7g.8**: the desktop "Ask…" composer, `conn.ask()` / `db.ask()` in the Python / Node / Go SDKs, the WASM SDK's split `db.askPrompt()` / `db.askParse()` shape (so the API key never enters the browser), and the MCP `ask` tool exposed by `sqlrite-mcp` (so any LLM agent over MCP can call `ask` against your database directly). See `docs/phase-7-plan.md` §7g for the full surface plan.

*crunchy-proxy* is a minimal PostgreSQL-aware proxy used to handle PostgreSQL application requests. The diagram below depicts a PostgreSQL client application connecting to the *crunchy-proxy*, which appears to the PostgreSQL application as any other PostgreSQL database connection. The *crunchy-proxy* accepts the inbound client requests, and routes them to an appropriate PostgreSQL cluster member (as described in more detail below).

One of the key features of the *crunchy-proxy* is the ability to route different SQL statements to a PostgreSQL cluster members based on certain pre-defined rules. This capability enables end-user applications to see a PostgreSQL cluster as a single connection. In order to support this capability, it is necessary that *crunchy-proxy* have knowledge of the SQL statements that a PostgreSQL application sends to PostgreSQL.

One approach to addressing the requirement that a proxy be "SQL aware" (e.g. link:http://www.pgpool.net/mediawiki/index.php/Main_Page[pgpool]) is to first parse each SQL statement looking for grammar that would imply a *write* or *update* and to then send those SQL statements to the cluster master. SQL statements that are determined to be *read-only* in nature are deemed safe to send to the cluster replica members. Remember, in PostgreSQL cluster replica members are only able to process SQL that is *read-only* in nature.

In taking this approach, *crunchy-proxy* has assumed (1) a user has access to their application's SQL and (2) a user has the ability to add the annotation in their SQL statements. If they do, then they can use the *crunchy-proxy* for SQL routing.

Of course these assumptions introduce certain limitations on the *crunchy-proxy*. Nonetheless, it was determined that these assumptions will not be unduly limiting in the usability of the *crunchy-proxy* and that the resulting limiations are justified by the benefits of (1) reduction in complexity associated with SQL parsing implementation, (2) increase in proxy throughput and (3) improved routing accuracy of the SQL parsing.

- The target calendar can carry the copy. This is true in three cases. The copy landed on the server already, and it has no unsent edit in a read-only calendar. The target is a local calendar. The target is linked and writable, and the organizer gate does not hold the copy back.

- Then use `--pick local`. It imports your recorded version over those rows and closes the conflict as `cancelled`. The source calendar gets no server object, so the next sync creates the item there. A read-only source calendar refuses this pick.
- This pick asks the server first whether the source object is gone. When the server cannot be reached, the pick refuses and changes nothing. Try again when the server answers.

- The target calendar cannot carry the copy. Both picks refuse, and the conflict stays open. Make the target writable, or move the item to another calendar.
- `abandoned`: the moved copy is gone (deleted before a pick). Both picks refuse. Restore the copy from the trash and move it again.

- `detached`: an unlink of the source calendar ended the move. The source has no pending delete any more, so the move cannot finish. Both picks refuse. Move the item again. A `cancel-failed` move also becomes `detached`, because its replay cannot reach a server after the unlink. A `sync reset` of the source does not end a move. - `cancel-failed`: the cancel moved the item back, and the import of the server version failed. `--pick server` runs the import again. `--pick local` restores your recorded version.

- For KV stores, there are more use cases that can accept this _slightly_ relaxed durability model than not. of course this isn't the case for a main DB, but KV stores often handle derived data, caches, or state that can be rebuilt.
That said, for cases needing stronger durability, you can call `store.flush()` after critical operations - gives you fsync-level guarantees.
The philosophy is: make the fast path really fast for those who need it, but provide escape hatches for stronger guarantees when needed.
- The real value isn't just raw speed - it's efficiency.

When operations complete in 200ns instead of blocking for microseconds/milliseconds on fsync, you avoid thread pool exhaustion and connection queueing. Each sync operation blocks that thread until disk confirms - tying up memory, connection slots, and causing tail latency spikes.
- Operations return immediately, threads stay available
- Background workers batch writes, amortizing sync costs across many operations
- Same hardware can handle 100x more concurrent requests
- Lower cloud bills from needing fewer instances
For desktop apps, this means your KV store doesn't tie up threads that the UI needs. For servers, it means handling more users without scaling up.

The durability tradeoff makes sense when you realize most KV workloads are derived data that can be rebuilt. Why block threads and exhaust IOPS for fsync-level durability on data that doesn't need it?
- Writes accumulated and flushed in batches
- Optimal disk utilization with large sequential writes
- Async I/O without thread pool overhead
- Multiple updates to same key automatically merged
- Keeps hot data in memory after disk write

Many packages aim to ease usage of Python enumerations as model fields. Most were superseded when Django provided TextChoices and IntegerChoices types. The motivation for django-enum was to:
* Work with any Enum including those that do not derive from Django's TextChoices and IntegerChoices.
* Coerce fields to instances of the Enum type by default.
* Allow strict adherence to Enum values to be disabled.
* Integrate as fully as possible with Django's existing level of enum support.
* Support enum-properties to enable richer enumeration types. (A less awkward alternative to dataclass enumerations with more features)
* Support bit field queries using standard Python Flag enumerations.
* Be as simple and light-weight an extension to core Django as possible.
* Enforce enumeration value consistency at the database level using check constraints by default.

django-enum provides a new model field type, EnumField, that allows you to treat almost any PEP435 enumeration as a database column. EnumField resolves the correct native Django field type for the given enumeration based on its value type and range. For example, IntegerChoices that contain values between 0 and 32767 become PositiveSmallIntegerField.
EnumField **is more than just an alias. The fields are now assignable and accessible as their enumeration type rather than by-value:**

Flag types are also seamlessly supported! This allows a database column to behave like a bit field and is an alternative to having multiple boolean columns. There are positive performance implications for using a bit field instead of booleans proportional on the size of the bit field and the types of queries you will run against it. For bit fields more than a few bits long the size reduction both speeds up queries and reduces the required storage space. See the documentation for discussion and benchmarks.

An agent proposes four things. rm -rf / is blocked and never runs. git push --force asks a human and runs once after approval. ls -la is allowed. An injected line in tool output is removed before the agent reads it.
|**When it acts**|After the tool ran|Before the tool runs, and again on its output|
|**A dangerous call**|Recorded|Blocked, or held for a human|
|**Injected tool output**|Recorded|Quarantined before the agent reads it|

An agent proposes a tool call. Inside the enforcement boundary it is decided, run at most once, inspected and recorded. A denied call goes to blocked and the tool never runs. The tool talks to the outside world only in the run step, and the sanitized result returns to the agent.

Enforcing integrations (Python SDK, frameworks, Claude Code, MCP gateway) feed the enforcement plane of pipeline, approvals, emergency stop and output checks. It writes records to the evidence plane of store, Merkle seals, replay and verifier. Both use a shared REST API, dashboard, CLI and storage.

Ten steps in order: identity, control, threat analysis, RBAC, loops, intent, human approval when escalated, final stop check, run, inspect output. A block in steps one to six, a denied approval or a tripped stop ends in refused, and the tool body never runs. An unsafe result is withheld or sanitized. Opt-in stages are off by default.
|Private network access|`127.0.0.1` · RFC 1918 addresses|Escalated; blocked with no approval channel|
|Injected tool output|Instruction lines in a result|Quarantined|

Records are sealed every 200 records or 30 seconds per tenant into hash-chained Merkle segments. The head is anchored outside the store. A standalone verifier takes an exported bundle and the expected head and reports intact, or fails if evidence was edited, reordered or truncated.
> Evidence is written only when a ledger is configured. Records are integrity-protected once sealed, and an anchor must live where a store writer cannot change it. See docs/EVIDENCE_INTEGRITY.md.

A replay runner sends each recorded step to the model under test. Its tool actions are answered from recorded evidence and the real world is never contacted. The traces are compared and classified as identical replay, failure reproduced, model diverged, or not enough evidence.

Target system architecture. Execution cells send Actions to the enforcement node, which holds the gateways, the sandbox supervisor, the egress proxy, the enforcement kernel, the evidence writer and the control agent. The egress proxy is the only path to the untrusted world. The control plane exchanges evidence, policy, leases and approvals with the node, and independent verifiers receive bundles and signed checkpoints.
Execution lifecycle: no effect before a durable decision

The twelve-step lifecycle: propose, normalise, admit, authorize, evaluate state, consult advisors, combine, approve when required, record, execute, observe and verify, inspect and deliver. Failures end in one of four outcomes: refused and recorded; no grant and cell paused; killed and session halted; or result withheld.
Information flow: typed, labelled values only

Untrusted content and secret data go to a quarantined worker with no effect tools. It returns a typed value, whose schema and size are checked, to the planner context. Every effect the planner proposes passes a flow check before reaching egress destinations, tools with effects or other agents.
Emergency governance: one person stops, two people resume

Control states: running, suspended, locked down, stopped and recovering. One person can stop from any of the first three. Resuming, lifting a lockdown and leaving stopped each take two people, and recovering returns to running once checks pass.

Three deployments compared by layer. Workstation: OS cells, panoptisd user service, embedded control plane, SQLite. Self-hosted: OS or VM cells, a node per runner or worker, stateless API replicas, PostgreSQL and object store. Hosted multi-tenant: a VM cell per session, node pools per region, regional control planes, row-level security and per-tenant keys.

- 解决了 sqlcipher 解密超过 1 GiB 的数据库时报 `database disk image is malformed` 的问题。
此前 `nt_msg.db`、`group_msg_fts.db` 等大库会在导出中途中止，明文库缺少大部分数据。
现在解密时在临时副本上迁移锁页，源数据库不受影响；这一步需要 `openssl`。
使用了 QQDecrypt 中记录的方法。
> **原因:** QQ 在数据库前附加了 1024 字节的明文文件头，SQLite 的锁区位于物理文件 1 GiB 处，因此 QQ 留空的是第 262144 页。
剥离文件头后，标准 SQLite 改认第 262145 页为锁页，而这一页存放着真实数据，读到即报错。
> **处理:** 找到引用第 262145 页的父页，把该页移到留空的第 262144 页，改写父页中的指针并重新计算两页的 HMAC，再由 sqlcipher 导出为标准布局的明文库。
> **限制:** 只支持锁页由内部页引用的情形，已知的真实样本均属于这种情形。
锁页为表或索引的根页、位于溢出链或被多处引用时，该数据库放弃导出并输出原因。
> **空间:** 剥头副本与导出中的数据库放在输出目录下的隐藏临时目录，结束后删除。
解密时输出目录约需源库两倍的可用空间，复制前会检查能否放下临时副本。

Pure-Go port of Yjs, the CRDT framework for collaborative applications, listed on the ports page of the Yjs documentation.

Ygo speaks the **Yjs V1 and V2 wire formats** byte for byte, apart from object key order, whole-number floats set from Go and a format attribute set to undefined (see Strings and values). The encoding is verified in both directions through **307 cross-language fixture scenarios** generated from `yjs@13.6.33`. The bundled WebSocket server speaks the `y-websocket` protocol: JavaScript clients using `y-websocket` connect to it directly, and the Go client connects to the reference `y-websocket` server. On `main` (unreleased), the server also serves `@hocuspocus/provider` 2.15, 3.4 and 4.8, and the Go client connects to Hocuspocus servers of those versions (see Hocuspocus setup). No CGO; `gomobile bind` produces an Android AAR (built in CI) and an iOS xcframework (built by hand).

- **Byte-level wire compatibility, verified in both directions.** 307 cross-language fixture scenarios (generated from `yjs@13.6.33`) cover the V1 and V2 update formats, snapshots, subdocuments, undo, observers, relative positions, GC, awareness, the sync protocol, and the Any values JavaScript has and Go does not (undefined, BigInt, -0), JS to Go and Go to JS, plus 56 lib0 primitive vectors. The suite runs in CI on every push to `main` and every pull request, so a regression in either direction fails the build. The exceptions are the Any values listed under Strings and values.

- **Pure Go, no CGO.** The CRDT core, the sync client and the server compile with `CGO_ENABLED=0` for all 47 targets in `go tool dist list`, `js/wasm` and `wasip1/wasm` included. The SQLite-backed store in `persist/sqlite`, and with it `yserve`, builds only where `modernc.org/sqlite` does: not on wasm, AIX, DragonFly, illumos, Plan 9, Solaris, MIPS or big-endian ppc64 Linux, NetBSD other than amd64, or OpenBSD other than amd64 and arm64. Elsewhere, supply your own `persist.Store` (it is a seven-method interface). `gomobile bind` produces an Android AAR (built in CI on every push to `main` and every pull request) and an iOS xcframework (built by hand on 2026-11-10) carrying a full mobile SDK: editable Text / Map, undo, cursors, and a built-in background sync client (WebSocket + reconnect), so a Swift / Kotlin app only renders UI. No V8, no embedded JavaScript engine, no Rust FFI bridge.

- **Embeddable sync client, offline-first.** The `client` package is a Go-native `y-websocket` provider, and with `Options.Hocuspocus` a Hocuspocus one: handshake, incremental updates, awareness, reconnect with backoff, and a liveness check that redials a connection which went silent. With a `LocalStore` it persists the document to disk (pure-Go SQLite), loads it before any network so the app works offline, and syncs edits made offline up on reconnect. The building block for bots, CLI tools, server-side agents, and the mobile SDK (`EnableOfflineStore`).

- **Ready-to-run server: yserve.** A self-hosted Yjs server in one binary, with no Node and no Redis. `y-websocket` clients connect unchanged (CI runs y-websocket 2.1 and 3.1 against it), and SQLite persistence and periodic document versioning are built in. The document is the URL path, slashes included; behind a proxy that keeps a path prefix, pass it as `-path-prefix`. It also embeds as a plain `http.Handler` inside an existing Go backend.

- **Scales horizontally, as a library.** Several instances of the `server` package behind a load balancer converge on the same document through a pluggable backplane: edits and live cursors both cross instances, so two users on different servers collaborate as if on one. An in-process hub ships in the core; an opt-in NATS adapter (a separate module, so NATS stays out of the core's dependencies) spans machines, with a JetStream mode that resumes delivery across a broker reconnect or restart. Clustered instances share one `Store` and run the same ygo version. The `yserve` binary has no backplane option.

- **Federated transport over Matrix.** An opt-in Matrix transport (a separate module, so mautrix stays out of a build that only wants the CRDT) turns an ordinary unencrypted Matrix room into the sync channel: peers publish updates as `dev.ygo.update` room events and merge what they read back, with no ygo server involved. A room is an append-only log with no ordering or exactly-once guarantee, which is exactly what Yjs updates tolerate. Room content is treated as untrusted — validated on both sides, decoded one event at a time so one bad event cannot break a whole page, encrypted rooms refused rather than silently written in the clear — though, as the module README spells out, Yjs updates do not authenticate deletes, so room membership is write access to the document. Exercised in CI against a real Dendrite on every push to `main` and every pull request. Its limits are documented rather than papered over.
